question_en: A company reporting under US GAAP has deferred tax assets that exceed deferred tax liabilities. All else equal, a reduction in the tax rate will most likely increase the company's:
option_a: operating profit.
option_b: debt-to-asset ratio.
option_c: shareholders' equity.
explanation_en:
Deferred tax asset vs. deferred tax liability
Income tax expense < taxes payable
Deferred tax asset
Created by overpaying tax in current period
Income tax expense > taxes payable
Deferred tax liability
Created by underpaying tax in current period
Deferred tax items (ie, deferred tax assets and liabilities) arise from the difference between income tax expense (for accounting purposes) and
taxes payable (for tax reporting) for a period. Differences can occur as tax expense is calculated according to accounting standards whereas
taxes payable are calculated according to the tax code.
Deferred tax assets (DTA) arise when taxable profit is greater than accounting profit and taxes payable are greater than tax expense.
Deferred tax liabilities (DTL) arise when taxable profit is less than accounting profit and taxes payable are less than tax expense.
In this scenario, the value of deferred tax items is directly correlated with the tax rate. All else equal, when the tax rate decreases (as is the
case in this scenario), DTA and DTL decrease. Since the company's DTA exceeds its DTL, it has a net DTA balance, which is reported as a net
long-term asset under US GAAP. Therefore, a decrease in the tax rate ultimately reduces total assets, which increases the debt-to-asset
(debt/asset) ratio.
(Choice A) Operating profit is pre-tax, so a decrease in tax expense will not affect operating profit.
(Choice C) Since the company has a net DTA, decreasing the tax rate also reduces the DTA. From the accounting equation assets = liabilities +
equity, equity would have to decrease, not increase, to maintain the balance.

question_en:
In 20X7, a firm:

- receives $10 million of payments in advance from a customer for goods to be delivered in 20X8. Assume the firm pays taxes on this amount in 20X7.
- is fined $5 million by the government. The firm pays the fine at the end of 20X7 and expenses it for accounting purposes. The fine is not deductible for tax purposes under the jurisdiction.

Based on this information, in 20X7, the carrying amount of liabilities is most likely:
option_a: equal to its tax base.
option_b: $5 million more than its tax base.
option_c: $10 million more than its tax base.
explanation_en:
The carrying amount of a liability reflects the reported book value on the balance sheet according to the applicable accounting standards. The
tax base of a liability reflects its value for tax purposes. Differences between accounting standards and tax codes may cause the carrying
amount to differ from the tax base. These temporary differences are reflected in deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities.
In this scenario, the carrying amount and tax base of each liability is calculated to determine the total difference in 20X7.
For accounting purposes, the firm cannot recognize the $10 million of customer advances as revenue until the goods are delivered in 20X8.
Therefore, it records $10 million as unearned revenue, a liability, in 20X7. In contrast, for tax purposes, the firm recognizes the $10 million
as taxable cash revenue in 20X7 and does not record a liability.
The firm pays the government fine in 20X7; therefore, the carrying amount is zero for accounting purposes. The fine is not tax deductible,
so the tax base is also zero.
In aggregate, the carrying amount of liabilities is $10 million more than the tax base.
(Choice A) The carrying amount would be equal to the tax base if the $10 million liability for unearned revenue were included in the tax base.
(Choice B) A carrying amount of $5 million more than the tax base results from incorrectly reporting a $5 million liability for fines in the tax base.

question_en: A company that reports under US GAAP presents its 20X3 deferred tax assets valuation allowance at $10,000. In 20X4, it is reported at $0. All else equal, the reduction in the valuation allowance most likely signals that the company expects:
option_a: higher taxes payable.
option_b: lower taxable income.
option_c: lower statutory tax rates.
explanation_en:
Deferred tax asset vs. deferred tax liability
Item created Accounting reporting Tax reporting
Deferred tax asset1 Income tax expense < Taxes payable
Deferred tax liability2 Income tax expense > Taxes payable
1Overpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax asset
2Underpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax liability
Deferred taxes account for temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable. Such differences occur due to differences
between tax calculations and financial statement reporting. A deferred tax asset (DTA) is created when a company pays more taxes (ie, tax
reporting) than it reports (ie, financial reporting). The DTA can offset (ie, be applied to) future taxes owed.
However, the company must expect the future taxes that the DTA will offset. To generate future taxes, the company must have taxable income.
If lower taxes are expected, the use of DTA is less likely, so its value is less likely to be realized. Under US GAAP, the company then decreases
the net DTA by increasing the valuation allowance (ie, contra account).
If taxable income and taxes payable are expected to increase, the DTA becomes more valuable. The company then lowers the valuation
allowance, which increases the net value of the DTA. In this scenario, the company reduces the valuation allowance to zero. This indicates that
the company's taxable income and taxes payable increased so much that the value of its DTA will be fully realized.
(Choices B and C) If taxable income or statutory tax rates are expected to be lower, the company can anticipate lower taxes payable and the
probability that it will use less, not more, of the DTA. To reflect decreased net DTA value, the valuation allowance is increased.

question_en: A company reports financial results using IFRS. Which of the following most likely represents a conservative accounting choice?
option_a: Assuming longer useful lives for noncurrent assets
option_b: Increasing life expectancies for retired pension recipients
option_c: Reducing the allowance for uncollectible accounts receivable
explanation_en: Comparison of common accounting choices Aggressive accounting Conservative accounting Recognizing revenue upon sale rather than when completely earned Not recognizing revenue while seller retains any risk Maintaining reserves so earnings can be "smoothed" across periods Electing shorter useful lives for noncurrent assets Using straight-line depreciation Using higher estimates for bad debt and warranty expense Conservative accounting is an important characteristic of high-quality financial reporting. Conservative choices represent the managerial philosophy that presenting financial results in a "worst-case" light minimizes the chances of future negative surprises. A defined benefit plan often represents a significant long-term liability based on projections that may never be realized. When a company assumes its employees will live longer in retirement, it acknowledges that it will likely owe them more money than originally anticipated. Increasing the liability signals that the company is making appropriate provisions today to cover higher obligations in the future. This is an example of a conservative accounting choice. By contrast, assuming longer useful lives for noncurrent assets or reducing the allowance for uncollectible accounts receivable decreases the current period's expenses and increases earnings (Choices A and C). Accounting choices that increase the current period's earnings are considered more aggressive.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the quality of financial reports and the quality of earnings?
option_a: High quality of earnings indicates a high quality of financial reporting.
option_b: Low quality of earnings prevents analysts from determining the quality of reporting.
option_c: High quality of financial reporting allows analysts to determine the quality of earnings.
explanation_en: The overall quality of financial statements varies widely (ie, exists on a spectrum) since it is a combination of earnings quality and reporting quality. Earnings quality is based on the sustainability and amount of earnings. Reporting quality is based on the usefulness of the financial information, as defined by its relevance and faithful representation. If a company complies with US GAAP or IFRS and follows the International Accounting Standards Board's Conceptual Framework, the quality of financial reporting should be high. High-quality reporting allows analysts to determine earnings quality. However, if management aggressively manipulates the rules (ie, earnings management), then reporting quality declines. At a certain point, the quality of reporting can be so low that assessing the quality of earnings is impossible: The report does not represent the company's performance and may be fraudulent. (Choice A) High earnings quality indicates that earnings are high and sustainable. Reporting quality is based on the information's usefulness. High or low earnings quality does not directly impact the reporting quality. (Choice B) Low earnings quality does not prevent analysts from determining the reporting quality. Management's compliance with accounting standards and the guidelines for preparing useful information determines the reporting quality.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
question_en: .An analyst suspects a company of manipulating its financials. A trend that could most likely be a warning sign is:
option_a: declining inventory turnover over multiple periods.
option_b: receivables decreasing as a percentage of total revenue.
option_c: a net-income-to-cash-from-operating-activities ratio consistently below 1.
explanation_en: Low-quality financial statements refer to statements that may be incomplete, biased and/or contain errors. The CFA Institute identifies three conditions that often lead to low-quality statements: motivation, opportunity, and rationalization. Both incorrect answers illustrate situations in which a company's decision makers could be motivated to present their company's financial situation in a way that distorts the true picture. Management can be motivated by career or compensation concerns to reduce earnings volatility (Choice B). One way to manage earnings volatility is to create reserves that management can draw on when needed to "smooth" earnings from period to period. A company with less volatile earnings in a volatile environment could be perceived as a superior investment, which in turn could lead to management having better job security and compensation. Similarly, a CEO's motivation for wanting to sell the company (Choice C) could be related to compensation. Many senior executives receive some of their compensation in company stock. Selling the company at a substantial premium directly benefits them, and companies with high earnings tend to command a higher price in takeovers. This could lead to choices that boost current earnings but prove to be unsustainable in the long term. By contrast, a company having a strong period has no need to further enhance earnings. It would want to issue high quality statements so that users would trust that the earnings are "real."

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following circumstances would least likely result in a company issuing financial reports considered to be of low quality?
option_a: The company is experiencing an exceptionally strong period.
option_b: Earnings are volatile from period to period due to a competitive industry.
option_c: The CEO wants to sell the company at a large premium to its current stock price.
explanation_en: Aggressive accounting vs. conservative accounting Aggressive Conservative Capitalizing costs Expensing costs Classifying investments as trading Classifying investments as available- securities for-sale securities Presenting better pro forma results Presenting pro forma results close to than IFRS or GAAP results IFRS or GAAP results Accounting choices affect the quality of a company's financial results. Aggressive accounting choices tend to inflate financial performance (eg, earnings, cash flow) in the current period but may understate performance in future periods. Conservative choices typically understate performance in the current period but may enhance future performance. Capitalizing (instead of expensing) in-process research and development (R&D) costs in a reporting period assigns those costs to an asset on the balance sheet. They are then amortized periodically as an expense on the income statement. The capitalization of a cost will produce: higher net income in the current period since the entire cost is not expensed immediately, but lower net income in future periods since the remaining cost is expensed over time. Therefore, capitalization is an aggressive accounting choice. R&D costs should be capitalized only when the product is reasonably certain to generate future revenue and is no longer considered to be in process. (Choice A) Pro forma earnings typically include numerous management adjustments (ie, add-backs) that cause them to differ from reported earnings (ie, those under GAAP or IFRS). In general, management presents pro forma earnings that are higher than reported earnings and therefore considered aggressive. (Choice C) When bond investments are treated as available-for-sale securities, any gains in fair value are included in other comprehensive income on the balance sheet instead of going directly to net income (earnings). Therefore, this treatment is a conservative choice.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
question_en: Adjusted EBITDA most accurately:
option_a: may exclude the impact of equity-based compensation.
option_b: may be impacted by the choice of depreciation method.
option_c: is commonly prepared under the same methodology across firms.
explanation_en: Primary mechanisms that enhance financial reporting discipline Regulators Recognize and enforce disclosure standards applicable to all companies Opinions that statements comply with standards and fairly present the Auditors company's finanical condition Features such as debt covenants create special financial reporting Investors requirements to aid creditors Many jurisdictions require a company's statements to be audited by an independent auditor. An unqualified (ie, "clean") auditor's opinion does not guarantee the statements' accuracy, but it certifies that the statements comply with accounting standards and present the company's results fairly. The prospect of a poor auditor's opinion can induce a company to produce high-quality statements since market repercussions from a poor report are severe. The company being audited pays the auditor's fee. By itself, that does not impugn an auditor's independence and objectivity. However, an auditor that bundles auditing with other services as part of overall engagement is not "independent." Earning compensation from other services may cause an auditor to provide a lenient audit opinion to preserve those additional compensation sources. (Choice B) Investors or creditors may have legally enforceable rights against a company that violates the terms of an investment contract. An example is a lender that can accelerate payment of the loan if the borrower violates a debt covenant. (Choice C) Regulations often impose penalties on a company if its financial statements contain material misstatements or omit certain information. The possibility of penalties tends to enhance reporting discipline, regardless of whether the regulations require management to attest to the information's accuracy.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
question_en: An analyst gathers the following information on two competitors, concerning their differences in accounting methods. To facilitate proper financial comparison, the analyst should most appropriately:
option_a: adjust Company 2's gross book value of fixed assets.
option_b: reduce Company 1's net income for fair value investment gains.
option_c: reduce Company 1's amount of intangible assets by its goodwill balance.
explanation_en: High-quality financial earnings are characterized by sustainability over future periods. The quality of reported earnings tends to be positively correlated to the quality of the financial statements that chronicle those earnings. Companies with conservative accounting policies tend to generate high-quality earnings more often than companies with more aggressive reporting methods. The same applies for companies that make unbiased accounting choices. Pro forma statements are one characteristic of aggressive reporting. They selectively present limited information that makes current earnings appear stronger than might otherwise be justified. The selective nature of the information calls into question whether the earnings are sustainable. Pro forma presentations do not comply with either US GAAP or IFRS. Choosing shorter useful lives for noncurrent assets represents a conservative accounting choice (Choice C). The shorter lives result in higher depreciation expense each year. The increased expense means lower earnings. Also, shorter useful lives implicitly signal the company's intent to invest in its infrastructure to foster future earnings growth. (Choice B) Revenue is the primary driver of earnings. Robust and sustainable revenues tend to result in consistent, high-quality earnings.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following reporting practices is most likely considered aggressive accounting?
option_a: Presenting pro forma earnings per share (EPS) that are lower than reported EPS.
option_b: Capitalizing, instead of expensing, in-process research and development (R&D) costs.
option_c: Using the criteria of available-for-sale securities, rather than trading securities, to treat bond
explanation_en: Under both IFRS and US GAAP, revenue can be recognized when the risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to the buyer. When goods are in transit: under Free on Board (FOB) destination, ownership transfers to the buyer when the shipped goods are received. Therefore, the seller can recognize revenue only when the goods arrive at the customer's destination. under FOB shipping point, ownership transfers to the buyer upon shipment. Therefore, the seller can recognize revenue when the goods are shipped. For a seller, switching shipping terms from FOB destination to FOB shipping will change the timing of when the goods' ownership is transferred, thus changing when revenue can be recognized. It effectively allows a seller to recognize revenue earlier, which results in more reported revenue for the current period. Therefore, management sometimes uses this tactic to enhance reported revenue for a period. (Choice A) Expensing, rather than capitalizing, an asset purchase will increase operating expenses for the current period, thus lowering profits. Expensing an asset purchase is a conservative choice. (Choice B) Decreasing future cash benefit projections in a goodwill impairment test will more likely lead to a write-down; therefore, it is a conservative choice.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following is least likely to increase financial reporting discipline?
option_a: Auditor reports included as part of the auditing company's consulting services
option_b: Debt covenants that require the current ratio to be at or above a minimum figure
option_c: Regulations that enforce disclosure but do not require management to certify financial
explanation_en: Common warning signs of accounting manipulation Frequent reporting "surprises" "Nonrecurring" items that consistently appear in multiple periods Unusual levels of receivables, payables, inventory turnover, operating cash flow, net income, profit margins Underestimating warranty expenses that are "restated" in subsequent periods Useful lives for long-term assets that are different than industry average Related-party transactions Heavy emphasis on pro forma (non-GAAP, non-IFRS) earnings Both GAAP and IFRS allow managers discretion over the financial information they are required to present and over how it is presented. Analysts must be vigilant to detect managers' manipulation of financial statements which may reduce the quality of the financial statements and/or the company's earnings, even if such manipulation is not so extreme as to be criminal conduct. Analysts should pay close attention to the ratio of cash from operations (CFO) to net income. Sales on credit (ie, new accounts receivable) are included in a company's net income. Receivables must be converted to cash to pay expenses. Not converting receivables to cash may indicate that the company is recognizing "sales" that are illusory (and thus cannot be converted to cash), which is an accounting impropriety. A ratio of at least 1.0 indicates that CFO is keeping pace with net income; a ratio of consistently less than 1.0 likely constitutes a warning sign. (Choice A) Inventory turnover (ie, the ratio of COGS to average inventory) measures how quickly a company sells its inventory. If this ratio is decreasing, it may signal that the company has poor inventory management or that its inventory is becoming obsolete. Declining inventory turnover is a warning sign. (Choice B) A bill-and-hold arrangement is an agreement for a sale today with delivery deferred to a subsequent period. The seller improperly recognizes the revenue today despite not delivering the goods. Consistently using bill-and-hold transactions to recognize revenue is a warning sign.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company reports a significant increase in earnings per share (EPS) for fiscal year 20X8. An analyst examining the annual financial statements determines that the increase arises mostly from sales of noncore fixed assets. The statements are GAAP-compliant in all respects, and the footnotes provide significant details about the sales. The financial statements most likely represent:
option_a: high-quality financial reporting and financial earnings.
option_b: high-quality financial reporting but low-quality financial earnings.
option_c: low-quality financial reporting but high-quality financial earnings.
explanation_en: Common warning signs of management manipulation Timing of revenue, vague service contracts, quarterly reporting surprises Misclassification of recurring and nonrecurring items Unusual levels of working capital, operating cash flow, profit margins Underestimation of rebates and warranty expenses or uncollectible accounts Depreciation choices (eg, modified useful lives, capitalizing instead of expensing) Related party transactions Lack of financial disclosure Heavy emphasis on pro forma (ie, non-GAAP, non-IFRS) earnings Management can intentionally misclassify recurring and/or nonrecurring items to manipulate financial results. This leads to poor reporting quality since the reported levels of operating performance are unlikely to be sustainable. Common manipulative practices include misclassifying: nonrecurring income as recurring (eg, reporting gains from asset disposals under operating income) (Choice A) and recurring expenses as nonrecurring (eg, reporting recurring restructuring charges as nonrecurring or unusual). In this question, classifying a loss from a rare lawsuit as nonoperating income is reasonable since a rare lawsuit is unlikely to recur. Therefore, such reporting would not be considered an attempt at manipulation. (Choice C) Receivables increasing at a much faster rate than revenues suggests less efficient receivables collection but may also signal aggressive "channel stuffing," which is a form of manipulation.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
question_en: High-quality financial earnings are least likely characterized by:
option_a: detailed pro forma financial statements.
option_b: sustainable and robust sources of revenue.
option_c: conservative estimates of useful lives for noncurrent assets.
explanation_en: Comparison of common accounting choices Aggressive accounting Conservative accounting Recognizing revenue upon sale rather than when completely earned Not recognizing revenue while seller retains any risk Maintaining reserves so earnings can be "smoothed" across periods Electing shorter useful lives for noncurrent assets Using straight-line depreciation Using higher estimates for bad debt and warranty expense Aggressive accounting choices tend to enhance current earnings or a company's financial position but decrease future earnings. In many cases, accounting standards and/or regulations present several options from which companies may select for a given situation. Aggressive accounting selects the choice that makes the company look best in the current period. Conservative accounting choices focus on the company's long-term outlook. When presented with viable options, managers that adhere to conservative accounting practices choose the one it believes best reflects the company's long-term earnings or financial position. A conservative choice can also represent what management determines is the more objective result. The percentage-of-completion method recognizes revenue proportionately to the expenses incurred each period for a multi-period construction contract. It assumes both that the company will likely be paid AND that expenses will not change materially during the contract. By contrast, the completed contract method is more conservative since no revenue, expenses, or earnings are recognized until the contract is completed. (Choices A and C) Increasing an estimate for bad debt expense is considered a conservative choice since it reduces earnings in the period of increase. Similarly, it is conservative to assume increases in compensation when determining a company's liability for a defined benefit plan since higher compensation causes the future liability to increase.

question_en: A company sells a homogeneous product and many of its sales are on credit. An analyst is reviewing the company's financial statements for the past three years. Which of the following would an analyst least appropriately consider to be a warning sign concerning the company's financial reporting?
option_a: Inventory turnover has declined each year over the period.
option_b: The company routinely recognizes revenue using bill-and-hold arrangements.
option_c: The ratio of cash flow from operations to net income is consistently more than 1.0.
explanation_en: Analysts and investors often pay close attention to net cash from operating activities (CFO) on the cash flow statement. The CFO section explains how cash is generated from core business activities by listing the sources and uses (ie, inflows and outflows) of cash. Management can manipulate CFO by delaying payment to suppliers, a tactic known as stretching payables. This makes CFO temporarily appear higher on a reporting date. For example, a EUR 10,000 invoice is due on December 31 of this year. A company can postpone payment by one day, to January 1 of next year, so that CFO appears to be EUR 10,000 higher on the year-end cash flow statement for this year. Trends such as decreasing accounts payable turnover ratios and an increasing number of days of payables outstanding may indicate the stretching of payables. (Choice B) Expensing, instead of capitalizing, asset costs decreases CFO since total asset costs are expensed on the income statement and are therefore captured in CFO. Conversely, capitalizing an asset moves asset costs to the balance sheet and decreases cash from investing activities. (Choice C) Proceeds from disposing capital assets are recognized as cash from investing activities. Gains from the disposal of assets do not increase CFO.

question_en: A manager collects the following information (in USD) on a company that reports under US GAAP: The company has no inventory at the beginning of the year and 100 units in inventory at the end of the year. Management is under pressure to meet its year-end earnings target and is considering changing its accounting methods. Which change in inventory costing method is most likely to increase earnings?
option_a: LIFO to FIFO
option_b: Periodic weighted average to LIFO
option_c: FIFO to periodic weighted average
explanation_en:
LIFO vs. FIFO: impact on financial statements
Inventory costs COGS Profit
Increasing Higher Lower
LIFO
Decreasing Lower Higher
Increasing Lower Higher
FIFO
Decreasing Higher Lower
Analysts should be aware of how a change in accounting methods or estimates can be used to manage or manipulate earnings. Even when
permitted by accounting standards, such a change should be interpreted in the context of the company's performance.
When inventory costs are rising, changing inventory valuations to FIFO lowers COGS and increases earnings, since, under FIFO, the first
(lowest cost) purchases flow into COGS. LIFO, however, uses the last purchases (highest cost) to value COGS, and under the periodic weighted
average (PWA) method, the average purchase cost flows into COGS.
Using the COGS formula, there are 100 units sold (0 + 200 − 100 = 100) during the period; the value of the units sold depends on the inventory
costing method used. To determine which change in accounting method increases earnings the most, first find COGS using each method.

question_en: Which of the following is most likely considered a warning sign in a company's financial reporting?
option_a: Classification of substantial expenses as recurring
option_b: Substantially exceeding fourth-quarter earnings guidance regularly
option_c: Increasing trend in levels of operating cash flow relative to net income
explanation_en:
Common warning signs of management manipulation
Timing of revenue, vague service contracts, quarterly reporting surprises
Misclassification of recurring and nonrecurring items
Unusual levels of receivables, payables, inventory turnover, operating cash flow, net income, profit margins
Underestimation of rebates and warranty expenses or uncollectible accounts
Depreciation issues (eg, modified useful lives, capitalizing instead of expensing)
Related party transactions
Lack of financial disclosure
Heavy emphasis on pro forma (non-GAAP, non-IFRS) earnings
Frequent fourth-quarter positive earnings surprises (ie, when earnings exceed guidance or estimates) may indicate that management is
manipulating profits or purposely providing unrealistic guidance. In essence, management may manipulate the timing of recognizing certain
revenues and expenses to achieve the desired outcome.
(Choice A) Classifying substantial expenses as recurring indicates conservatism in management's choice of reporting since it lowers profits.
Management typically manipulates reporting to show higher profits.
(Choice C) Increasing levels of operating cash flow to net income indicate high-quality net income since there are high levels of cash that support
income that is accrued.

question_en: Which of the following actions taken by management can most likely mislead investors by improving the appearance of net cash from operating activities?
option_a: Delaying payment to suppliers
option_b: Expensing instead of capitalizing asset costs
option_c: Disposing of outdated capital equipment at a gain
explanation_en:
Analysts and investors often pay close attention to net cash from operating activities (CFO) on the cash flow statement. The CFO section explains
how cash is generated from core business activities by listing the sources and uses (ie, inflows and outflows) of cash. Management can
manipulate CFO by delaying payment to suppliers, a tactic known as stretching payables. This makes CFO temporarily appear higher on a
reporting date.
For example, a EUR 10,000 invoice is due on December 31 of this year. A company can postpone payment by one day, to January 1 of next year,
so that CFO appears to be EUR 10,000 higher on the year-end cash flow statement for this year. Trends such as decreasing accounts payable
turnover ratios and an increasing number of days of payables outstanding may indicate the stretching of payables.
(Choice B) Expensing, instead of capitalizing, asset costs decreases CFO since total asset costs are expensed on the income statement and are
therefore captured in CFO. Conversely, capitalizing an asset moves asset costs to the balance sheet and decreases cash from investing
activities.
(Choice C) Proceeds from disposing capital assets are recognized as cash from investing activities. Gains from the disposal of assets do not
increase CFO.
